1.title: CDMP FUNDAMENTALS
1.text: Welcome to Module 2: Data Handling Ethics. This is Chapter 2 of the DMBOK. Like the previous chapter, it carries only about two percent of the exam, but the concepts here are increasingly important in the real world — and the exam does test a handful of precise facts, especially around privacy law and bias. So let's make these few questions easy points.

1.title: Module Overview & Learning Objectives
1.text: Here's our roadmap for this module. You'll learn the formal definition of data handling ethics — and you'll notice it includes the phrase "community responsibility," which matters. You'll master the three core concepts and the Belmont principles that data ethics borrows from medicine. You'll be able to list the seven GDPR principles and contrast GDPR with Canada's PIPEDA and the US FTC criteria. You'll learn the crucial distinction between a data controller and a data processor. And you'll understand the major risks of unethical data handling — bias, data snooping, misleading visualizations — and how an organization builds an ethical data culture. Let's begin.

1.title: What Is Data Handling Ethics?
1.text: Let's define our terms. Ethics, simply put, are principles of behavior based on ideas of right and wrong — things like fairness, respect, integrity, transparency, and trust. Now the DMBOK definition you should memorize: data handling ethics are concerned with how to procure, store, manage, interpret, analyze or apply, and dispose of data in ways aligned with ethical principles — including community responsibility. That last phrase is doing real work. It tells you that your ethical obligations don't stop at the edge of your organization; they extend to the wider community and society. And notice that this responsibility runs across the entire data lifecycle, from creation all the way to destruction. So when the exam tests the definition, remember those two ideas: community responsibility, and the full lifecycle.

1.title: Business Drivers
1.text: Why should an organization care about data ethics beyond just following the law? The DMBOK borrows a line of thinking from the quality guru W. Edwards Deming: ethics means doing it right when no one is looking. Increasingly, ethical data handling is recognized as a genuine competitive business advantage — it increases the trustworthiness of the organization and its data, which strengthens relationships with customers and stakeholders. The primary practical reason, though, is risk reduction: to reduce the chance that data gets misused by employees, customers, or partners. You'll see a cluster of executive roles emerge to manage this risk — the Chief Data Officer, Chief Risk Officer, Chief Privacy Officer, and Chief Analytics Officer. And here's an exam-worthy fact: holding the CDMP certification itself requires you to subscribe to a formal code of ethics — including an obligation to handle data ethically for the good of society, beyond just the company that employs you.

1.title: Three Core Concepts of Data Ethics
1.text: The ethics of data handling, however complex, center on three core concepts — and the exam likes to test them as a set. First, impact on people: because data represents real individuals and drives decisions that affect their lives, we have an imperative to manage its quality and reliability. Second, potential for misuse: misusing data can harm both people and organizations, so there's an ethical imperative to prevent that misuse. And third, the economic value of data: data has real economic value, and the ethics of data ownership should determine how that value is accessed, and by whom. Impact on people, potential for misuse, economic value — three concepts, easy to remember.

1.title: Ethical Principles — The Belmont Report
1.text: Where do data ethics principles come from? Interestingly, from medicine. The DMBOK adapts the tenets of bioethics — specifically the Belmont Report, published by the US Department of Health and Human Services in 1979 for medical research. Belmont gives us three principles — the pillars on screen. Respect for Persons: treat people with dignity and autonomy, take extra care with those who have diminished autonomy, and require informed, valid consent. Beneficence, which has two parts: first, do no harm; and second, maximize benefits while minimizing harms. And Justice: the fair and equitable treatment of people — which means watching out for algorithms that disproportionately benefit or harm a particular group. Later, the US Department of Homeland Security's Menlo Report adapted these for technology research and added a fourth principle: Respect for Law and Public Interest. For the exam: Belmont equals three principles, originally for medical research in 1979, and Menlo adds the fourth.

1.title: Principles Behind Data Privacy Law
1.text: Privacy law tries to codify these ethical principles, and it has a long history. Legal scholars Warren and Brandeis described privacy as a human right back in 1890. After the Second World War, the European Convention of Human Rights in 1950 established both a general right to privacy and a specific right to information privacy. Then, in 1980, the OECD established its Guidelines and Principles for Fair Information Processing — eight core principles covering things like collection limits, data quality, specified purpose, use limits, security safeguards, openness, the right to challenge accuracy, and accountability. Those eight principles became the foundation for the European Union's data protection laws. Here's the key exam point: the OECD principles have since been superseded by the principles underlying the GDPR. So OECD came first and laid the groundwork; GDPR replaced it.

1.title: The 7 GDPR Principles (EU, 2016)
1.text: The General Data Protection Regulation, the EU's landmark 2016 law, rests on seven principles, and you should know all seven. Fairness, lawfulness, and transparency — process data openly and legally. Purpose limitation — collect only for specified, explicit, legitimate purposes. Data minimization — collect only what's necessary. Accuracy — keep data correct and up to date, and rectify or erase errors without delay. Storage limitation — keep data no longer than necessary. Integrity and confidentiality — secure the data appropriately. And accountability — controllers must be able to demonstrate compliance. A useful exam tip: the GDPR also mandates Privacy by Design, meaning privacy protections must be built into systems from the very start, not bolted on afterward. Seven principles plus Privacy by Design — lock those in.

1.title: GDPR Roles, Rights & Consent
1.text: This slide covers some of the most heavily tested GDPR specifics, so pay close attention. First, two key roles, shown side by side on screen. The data controller is the party that determines the purposes and the means of processing personal data — in other words, the one who decides why and how. The data processor processes that data on behalf of, and strictly under the instructions of, the controller — a cloud storage vendor is the classic example. Next, individuals have rights: access, rectification, portability, the right to object, and the right to erasure, also called the right to be forgotten. And finally, consent — when processing relies on consent, that consent must be an affirmative action that is freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous. Silence or pre-ticked boxes don't count. The exam loves the controller-versus-processor distinction, so remember: the controller decides, the processor merely acts on instructions.

1.title: PIPEDA (Canada) & US FTC Criteria
1.text: Beyond GDPR, the DMBOK covers two more regimes. Canada's PIPEDA has nine principles: accountability, identifying purposes, consent, limiting collection use disclosure and retention, accuracy, safeguards, openness, individual access, and compliance challenges. One detail the exam likes: under PIPEDA, identifying purposes must happen at or before the time of collection. And in Canada, the Federal Privacy Commissioner handles complaints but only in an ombudsman role — meaning their decisions are recommendations, not legally binding. The United States takes a lighter-touch approach through the FTC's five criteria: notice and awareness, choice and consent, access and participation, integrity and security, and enforcement and redress. Here's a handy way to keep the counts straight: GDPR has seven, PIPEDA has nine, FTC has five, OECD had eight, and Belmont has three plus one. Memorize those numbers — they're easy exam points.

1.title: Online Data in an Ethical Context
1.text: The DMBOK highlights four recurring ethical topics specific to online data. First, ownership of data — who really controls your personal data when it's held by social media sites and data brokers who build deep profiles you may not even know exist. Second, the right to be forgotten — the ability to have information about you erased from the web, which ties into data retention practices. Third, identity — the right to expect a single, correct identity, and the option to maintain a private one. And fourth, freedom of speech online — the line between expressing opinions and harmful behavior like bullying, trolling, or incitement. Notice how the right to be forgotten connects directly back to GDPR's right to erasure — the same idea, viewed from the online-ethics angle.

1.title: Risks of Unethical Handling — Timing & Visualizations
1.text: Now let's look at how data gets misused, because understanding bad practice clarifies good practice. The classic reference here is Darrell Huff's 1954 book, How to Lie with Statistics. The DMBOK frames ethical handling as a positive duty — not just avoiding harm, but actively being truthful and transparent. The first risk category is timing. You can lie by omitting or including data points based on when you report. A concrete, illegal example is market timing — placing end-of-day stock trades to artificially inflate a stock's closing price. Business Intelligence staff are often the first to notice such anomalies, and they have an ethical duty to report them. The second category is misleading visualizations: changing the scale to exaggerate a trend, leaving out inconvenient data points, comparing unrelated facts, or breaking conventions — like a pie chart whose slices don't add up to one hundred percent.

1.title: Unclear Definitions & Data Snooping
1.text: The third risk category is unclear definitions and invalid comparisons. The DMBOK gives a memorable example: a report claiming 108.6 million people were on welfare while only 101.7 million had full-time jobs — making welfare look rampant. The catch? The two figures counted completely different things; the welfare number included everyone in a household where anyone received benefits. The ethical fix is simple: provide the context that informs meaning — clear, unambiguous definitions of the population you're measuring. Closely related is data snooping, sometimes called data dredging or fishing. This is where an analyst runs exhaustive correlations across a dataset until something looks statistically significant — but because of how statistical significance works, some of those results are purely random. It essentially over-trains the model and misleads the untrained. It's especially common in the financial and medical sectors. So: data snooping produces false significance from too many correlations.

1.title: Bias — The Five Types
1.text: Bias deserves its own slide because it's both important and testable. Bias is an inclination of outlook; in statistics, it means deviations from expected values, often from systematic errors in sampling or selection. Critically, bias can be introduced at any point in the data lifecycle — when data is collected, when it's selected for analysis, through the analysis methods themselves, or in how results are presented. The DMBOK names five types. One: collecting data for a pre-defined result. Two: biased use of data that was collected fairly. Three: hunch and search — using only the data that confirms your hunch. Four: biased sampling methodology — which you counter by using statistical tools to select samples. And five: context and culture — biases rooted in your own cultural viewpoint. The Justice principle creates a positive duty to actively watch for these biases, which matters most in large-scale processing that could affect groups historically subjected to prejudice.

1.title: Risks in Transforming & Integrating Data
1.text: When data moves and transforms between systems, integration introduces its own ethical risks — and these intersect with core data management problems. The DMBOK names four. First, limited knowledge of data's origin and lineage: if you don't know where data came from or how it changed, you can't prove it represents what you claim. Second, poor quality data: without measurable quality standards, you simply can't vouch for it. Third, unreliable Metadata: this leads to misunderstanding and misuse, which is why Metadata should carry provenance tags, ownership, and protection requirements — especially when data crosses borders. And fourth, no documentation of remediation history: here's the subtle point — even well-intentioned data fixes can be illegal, so all remediation must follow a formal, auditable change-control process.

1.title: Obfuscation & Redaction
1.text: Obfuscation and redaction mean making data anonymous or stripping out sensitive information. But — and this is the key exam point — obfuscation alone may not be sufficient, because a downstream activity, like further analysis or combining your data with other datasets, can re-identify the individuals you thought you'd protected. The DMBOK discusses three related practices. Data aggregation removes personal identifiers while keeping analytic value — for instance, rolling individual records up into geographic areas. Data marking classifies data by sensitivity — secret, confidential, personal — to control who it's released to. And data masking is a clever technique where only correct submitted responses unlock a process, and the operators themselves can't see the underlying data — think of an outsourced call center. Keep marking and masking straight: marking classifies sensitivity; masking hides the actual values while the data is still being used.

1.title: Building an Ethical Data Culture (4 Steps)
1.text: So how does an organization actually build an ethical data culture? It takes understanding your current practices, defining expected behaviors, codifying them, and providing training and oversight — all backed by strong leadership and a formal Organizational Change Management process. The DMBOK lays out four steps. Step one: review your current-state data-handling practices and connect them explicitly to ethical and compliance drivers. Step two: identify your principles, practices, and risk factors. Step three: create an ethical data-handling strategy and roadmap. And step four: adopt a socially responsible ethical risk model. The most testable piece here is the framework used in step two — a chain that goes Principle, then Risk, then Practice, then Control, exactly as the chevrons on screen show. For example: the principle that people have a right to health-data privacy; the risk that wide access exposes it; the practice of letting only care staff access it; and the control of an annual access review. Principle, Risk, Practice, Control.

1.title: Ethical Strategy Components & Governance
1.text: Let's flesh out that strategy and where governance fits. An ethical data-handling strategy includes values statements, ethical data-handling principles, a compliance framework, risk assessments, training and communications — which notably includes an annual ethics statement affirmation that employees sign — plus a roadmap and an approach to auditing and monitoring. The socially responsible risk model asks analytics projects to account for four things: how populations are selected for study, how data is captured, what the analytics will focus on, and how the results are made accessible. Now, who owns all this oversight? Data Governance, working with legal counsel. And the DMBOK is specific: Data Governance has a particular duty to review the plans and decisions proposed by BI, analytics, and Data Science studies. One last crucial point — automated monitoring alone is not sufficient. The analysts themselves must reflect on possible bias. Tools can't replace human ethical judgment.

1.title: Key Numbers & Quick Facts (Cheat Sheet)
1.text: Let's consolidate the testable facts for this chapter. There are three core concepts of data ethics. Belmont has three principles, with Menlo adding a fourth. GDPR has seven principles, PIPEDA has nine, the FTC has five, the OECD had eight — now superseded by GDPR — and the EDPS set out four pillars. There are five types of bias. The Belmont Report dates to 1979 and was written for medical research. How to Lie with Statistics is Darrell Huff, 1954. And privacy was established as a right in Europe by the European Convention of Human Rights in 1950. If a question hinges on a number, it's almost certainly on this slide — so drill it until it's automatic.

1.title: Common Exam Traps
1.text: Let me steer you around this chapter's traps. First: the Belmont Report was written for medical research in 1979, then adapted for data — don't let an answer claim it was originally about data. Second, the big one: the data controller decides the purpose and means, while the processor only acts on instructions; the exam constantly tries to swap these. Third: obfuscation does not fully protect data, because combining datasets can re-identify people. Fourth: data marking classifies sensitivity, while data masking hides the values during use — different practices. And fifth: automated monitoring is never enough on its own; people must reflect on bias. One more: keep the timeline straight — OECD came first in 1980 and was superseded by GDPR. Know these, and you'll avoid the usual stumbles.

1.title: Module Summary
1.text: Let's wrap up. Data handling ethics govern how we procure, manage, use, and dispose of data — including our responsibility to the wider community. The principles trace back to the Belmont Report's three tenets — Respect for Persons, Beneficence, and Justice — plus Menlo's fourth. In privacy law, the OECD's eight principles gave way to GDPR's seven, alongside Canada's PIPEDA with nine and the US FTC with five. The major risks of unethical handling are timing, misleading visuals, data snooping, the five types of bias, integration risks, and weak obfuscation. And you build an ethical culture through the chain Principle, Risk, Practice, Control — with Data Governance providing oversight, especially over BI, analytics, and Data Science. That's Chapter 2.

1.title: Let's Test Your Knowledge
1.text: Time for five practice questions on data handling ethics. Several of these turn on precise GDPR wording — particularly the controller-versus-processor distinction — so read each one carefully and commit to your answer before you reveal the solution. Here we go.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one: under GDPR, which party determines the purposes and means of processing? The answer is A, the data controller. The processor acts on instructions; the data subject is the individual; the data steward is a governance role.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two: a cloud vendor processing data strictly on a retailer's documented instructions is classified as what? The answer is A, a data processor. Handling or storing data doesn't make you a controller — control is about deciding the purpose and means, which stays with the retailer.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three asks about a positive duty in data ethics. The answer is D — actively using data to produce beneficial outcomes, not merely refraining from harm or meeting the legal minimum. A positive duty is about doing good, not just avoiding bad.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four: selling customer data to third parties most directly raises which ethical concern? The answer is C — whether customers gave informed consent for this secondary use and share equitably in the value. That ties to the economic-value-of-data concept and respect for persons. And

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: question five: the purpose of a data ethics committee? The answer is B — oversight and governance of the ethical implications of data practices. It doesn't replace security audits, legal review, or budgeting. That's Module 2. Next up, the heavy hitters begin — Module 3, Data Governance, one of the highest-weighted chapters on the exam. I'll see you there.
